Every page in the Notebook Chain was written by a scientist who tested an idea. Today's page is about a willow tree. Before you read it, make a prediction. The tree slice has ten pieces. Tap Soil, Water, Air, or Sunlight to fill each piece. Then write one reason. Your prediction is saved until Part 4.

Van Helmont measured carefully, and his numbers were right. But his idea, water alone, left out something that was around the tree the whole time. Good scientists can be careful and still miss something. That's why the chain keeps going.
I took a clay pot. I put in two hundred pounds of soil that I had dried in an oven, and I wet it with rainwater.
In it I planted a willow stem that weighed five pounds.
After exactly five years, the tree that grew weighed one hundred sixty-nine pounds and about three ounces.
Whenever it needed water, I gave it only rainwater or distilled, very clean, water.
The pot was big and set into the ground. To keep blowing dust out of the soil, I covered the top with a tin-coated iron plate full of small holes.
I did not count the weight of the leaves that fell off in the four autumns.
At the end, I dried the soil again. It weighed the same two hundred pounds, less about two ounces.
So one hundred sixty-four pounds of wood, bark, and roots had come from water alone.
This is Earth, seen from a million miles away.
Closer. Western Europe, from a satellite.
About 400 years ago, a scientist who lived near here planted a willow tree in a pot.
A grown willow can weigh more than a car. It all started as one small stem.
A tree like this has thousands of leaves.
Leaves are dotted with tiny openings called stomata. Air moves in and out here.
Inside the leaf are cells. The green dots are chloroplasts, where the plant makes its food.
And all around the leaf is air, full of gases too small to see.
A tiny seed grows into a giant tree. Where does all of that wood come from?
Organism. A living thing. A willow tree is an organism, and so are you.
Carbon dioxide. A gas in the air. Plants pull it in through tiny holes in their leaves.
Water. Plants take it in through their roots. Van Helmont gave his willow only rainwater.
Leaves. The plant parts that catch sunlight and pull in air for making food.
Roots. The plant parts under the ground. They pull water and nutrients out of the soil.
Producer. A living thing that makes its own food. Plants are producers.

This is a real page from seventeen seventy-two, by Joseph Priestley. Tap a yellow line to hear it in plain English. Then sort his sentences. Which one is his claim? Which ones are evidence? Then look for the reasoning. Priestley left that part out, so you'll pick it.
Now run Priestley's jars yourself. Before each step, make a prediction. A candle burns until it goes out. Then the mint goes in. Wait the days, and test both jars with a lit candle.
Here comes the other side. Press play on each quote. Then tap the evidence card that answers it best. One card is true, but it doesn't answer any of them.

Two more witnesses. First, predict what the carbon dioxide number will do in a sealed jar. Then run the jar in the light, and switch the light off. Watch the meter. After that, predict which tray of seedlings gains more mass.

Today you are the judge. Look at the lettuce in this photo. It grew to full size. Slide to show how many cups of soil you think it used up as it grew. Then write one reason. Your prediction is saved, and you'll find out the real answer in Part 3.

Priestley's page never says whether his jars sat in the light. Later, his test did not always work, and he could not tell why. The missing piece was light. Careful scientists can still leave something out. That's why the chain keeps going.
I found that candles burn very well in air where plants have grown for a long time. So I wondered if plants could also fix air that a burning candle had spoiled.
So on August seventeenth, seventeen seventy-one, I put a sprig of mint into air in which a wax candle had burned out.
On the twenty-seventh of the same month, another candle burned perfectly well in it.
I did this eight or ten times in the rest of the summer, and it worked every time.

Many times I split the spoiled air into two jars. I put the plant in one and left the other the same way, but with no plant. A candle always burned in the jar with the plant, and never in the other one.
When the plant was healthy, five or six days were usually enough to fix the air. Without a plant, I kept this air for many months, and it did not change at all.
On August 27, another candle burned perfectly well in the mint's jar.
These green dots are chloroplasts, packed inside the cells of a leaf. This is where a plant builds its food.
Zoom out. A lettuce leaf, made of millions of those cells.
This lettuce is being lifted out of its tray. Look at its long white roots. There is no soil anywhere.
Some farms grow lettuce like this, in rows of pipes filled with water.
Farther out. Farm fields, seen from space. Every green circle is a crop, growing bigger every day.
And all of it on one planet, wrapped in a thin layer of air.
Three different experiments, done in three different ways. Can they all point to the same answer about where a plant's mass comes from?
Plants eat soil. That's why their roots grow down into the dirt.
A tree gets its wood from the soil. Where else could all that wood come from?
Farmers add fertilizer, so fertilizer must be the plant's food.
Claim. A sentence that answers the question. It says what you think is true. For example: plants need light to grow.
Evidence. Data or observations that support a claim. Anyone should be able to check it. For example: the willow gained one hundred sixty-four pounds.
Reasoning. The explanation of why your evidence proves your claim. It connects the dots.
Misconception. An idea many people believe that the evidence does not support. For example: plants eat soil.
Carbon dioxide. A gas in the air. Plants take it in through their leaves and use it to build sugar.
Photosynthesis. How plants use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar for growing.

In seventeen twenty-four, Stephen Hales sealed a sunflower's pot under a sheet of lead and weighed it every morning and evening. On a sunny day, more than a pound of water left through the leaves. Hales wondered if air went in too. This week, you finish his picture. Build the sunflower, then show what goes in, what comes out, and what the plant builds.

No headset today? You can still make Plate seventeen. Follow one carbon atom from the air, and one bit of water from the soil, into Hales's sunflower. At each fork, pick the way it goes next. If you take a wrong turn, read the hint and try again. The route you finish is your evidence.
